AI tends to produce similar code for different users, so copied code gets flagged.
AI chatbots make unauthorized assistance easier and have raised cheating.
AI output is drawn from previously published work and is not original work.
Appropriate use of technology as an aid for learning counts as academic honesty.
Deviating from the AI heuristics does not automatically qualify as academic misconduct.
Copilot can almost fully autocomplete code when you start typing.

all|course|none|background.label: AI's costs to privacy, creators, workers and environment

items.directive: LLMs raise serious ethical issues, and AI misuse can harm others.
Powerful AI technology calls for caution and informed consent, and AI empowers bad actors.
AI tools store and analyze prompts and can leak confidential data.
AI-generated code is based on others' code and may come with licenses it does not carry over.
AI systems consume huge amounts of energy and water and create real resource costs.
AI training data is usually harvested from the internet without consent.
AI systems depend on moderation labor by human workers.

all|course|none|background.label: How employers and industry limit AI use

items.directive: Employers assess job candidates without AI, and interviews do not allow AI, so unaided skills matter.
Much of the software industry prohibits AI use because of serious concerns.

P72.01.directive: Provide students and advisors with contact information for human assistance, a list of campus resources and a designated referral point for help with AI, such as a peer program run by students with AI skills.
P72.01.why: The sources sit in AI guidance and one names AI directly ('a peer-to-peer program for students that taps into students with AI skill sets'); 'human assistance' is offered as the human alternative to AI help.

P139.01.directive: Adopt and apply the AI guidance and points to consider that the university recommends, for example to make AI cheating less necessary and less appealing.
P139.01.why: The guidance being adopted is the AI guidance itself: Lehigh says it should 'make AI "cheating" both less necessary and less appealing'; Pittsburgh and USC refer to their AI recommendations.

P69.09.directive: Findings of AI-related misconduct require a standard of proof, such as clear and convincing evidence or more likely than not, that AI or other unauthorized aid was used.
P69.09.why: William & Mary applies the standard to 'whether AI has been used to reach the threshold of proof', and UC Irvine to whether 'you did not personally complete an assignment', in AI guidance.

P69.15.directive: The burden of proof in academic misconduct cases lies with the university.
P69.15.why: Both sources state a general rule for all misconduct cases ('The burden of proof is on the university for all academic misconduct cases'), with no AI-specific content.

P71.06.directive: Provide channels for reporting concerns and AI-related ethical violations, correcting errors and seeking redress, and receive and review the reports.
P71.06.why: North Florida names the object: 'mechanisms for reporting and addressing AI-related ethical violations'; the other sources describe the same channels in AI governance documents.

P71.07.directive: Activate incident response for AI-related security incidents, document and investigate them, notify affected parties and regulators, and refer violations to proper bodies.
P71.07.why: Virginia Tech's source is 'Incident Response: AI-related security incident procedures'; the others describe the incident procedure in the same AI governance documents.

P60.06.directive: Ensure students do not feel policed.
P60.06.why: The only source says 'Students should not feel policed.' and names no AI tool, detector or AI-specific practice.

P68.09.directive: Develop and deploy educational modules to help students who commit violations.
P68.09.why: The source ('Educational modules should be developed and deployed to assist students with violations') concerns integrity violations in general and does not mention AI.

P137.03.directive: Retain applicable records and then destroy them in accordance with the state's records retention requirements.
P137.03.why: The source restates the state's general records rule ('Applicable records must be retained and then destroyed in accordance with the Commonwealth's Records Retention'), with nothing AI-specific.

P54.12.directive: If you serve on a designated body, recommend revisions or updates to the AI policy as legal, technological and regulatory requirements change.
P54.12.why: Purdue's source is 'Provide recommendations on policy changes regarding the use of AI'; Augusta and Santa Monica tie updates to 'updated regulatory requirements' and 'legal, technological, and regulatory developments'.

P99.12.directive: Most students who violate integrity rules do so out of stress, anxiety and academic pressure.
P99.12.why: The sources describe why students cheat in general ('Most students who commit violations do it out of stress'), not anything about AI.

CT09.c05.directive: Only course staff may provide solution-specific debugging assistance.
CT09.c05.why: The source ('Only the course staff may provide solution-specific debugging assistance.') is a general collaboration rule that names no AI tool.

CT38.c07.directive: You may review students' AI session transcripts.
CT38.c07.why: The source 'Staff may review transcripts' refers to the transcripts of students' AI chat sessions that the course's AI policy discusses.

P86.11.directive: When AI records or transcribes a meeting, balance productivity and convenience with respect for all participants' privacy, and treat the recordings as private among those who took part.
P86.11.why: Both Davidson sentences come from its guidance on AI meeting recording and transcription; 'productivity and convenience' is the benefit of those AI tools and 'considered private among those who participated' refers to their recordings.

P93.06.directive: Structure your AI prompts with elements such as a role or persona, task, context and format.
P93.06.why: The sources are about prompting AI: 'When writing an AI prompt, focus on persona, task, context and format' (Sam Houston State) and 'Assign a role to ChatGPT' (Santa Clara).

P93.13.directive: Learn prompt engineering for AI tools, including how to write clear, precise and iterative prompts that work.
P93.13.why: Prompt engineering is a skill for AI tools, and the sources say so ('Learning to use AI responsibly and ethically is an important skill', Pepperdine; 'clear, precise, and iterative prompts', North Dakota State).

P76.05.directive: Follow university communications standards and approval processes for public-facing and official materials made or edited with AI, such as photos.
P76.05.why: Buffalo's source applies the standards to 'Photos created or edited using AI for official UB purposes'; the others apply existing communications rules within AI guidance.

P117.07.directive: Verify that an AI tool has adequate security, such as encryption and secure data handling, and is appropriate for your data before using it.
P117.07.why: The sources describe checking the AI tools the guidance covers: 'Ensure the tool has robust security measures in place, such as encryption' (UNLV) and 'verify that the specific tool you are using is appropriate for your data' (Utah State).

P75.03.directive: Report suspicious messages and communications, and questionable AI output, to the designated IT or security office.
P75.03.why: Colby's source names AI: 'Report suspicious communications and questionable AI output to ITS.'; the others repeat the reporting duty inside AI guidance on phishing.

P71.10.directive: If you do research, report adverse events or unanticipated problems to the IRB.
P71.10.why: The source ('Researchers must report any adverse events or unanticipated problems to the IRB') is the general IRB reporting rule and does not mention AI.

P114.03.directive: If you are not linked to the university and cause damage through AI use, you alone answer for it, exonerating the university, and you are barred from using AI technology there.
P114.03.why: The source ('responderá exclusivamente por el daño causado , eximiendo y exonerando a la') is in the university's AI policy, and 'the technology' the person is barred from is the AI technology that policy governs.

P80.08.directive: Escalate denials, disputes and unresolved questions about AI use to a named committee, such as an AI governance committee, or to a leader or program head.
P80.08.why: Arkansas sends appeals to 'the AI Governance Committee' and Delaware asks people to raise questions 'as they pertain to the use of Generative AI'.

P52.16.directive: You keep ownership of your own prompts, work and course materials when you use AI tools.
P52.16.why: The sources are about AI tools: 'the person entering the prompts and text materials retains the copyright' (UAB) and 'your content is not used to train any models, and you retain ownership' (Portland CC).

CT02.c11.directive: Appropriate use of technology as an aid for learning counts as academic honesty.
CT02.c11.why: The source ('includes the appropriate use of technology as an aid for learning and productivity') is a general honesty statement about technology and does not mention AI.

inst.intro: The 102 university, school and department policies for staff and administrators sit mostly before the course, where 47 of them ask staff to vet AI tools, write AI policy and fund AI programs. Another 21 apply while students work and 19 over time, 7 apply when misuse is suspected and 1 at the start of the course, and 7 state background facts. By stance, Duties and facts is the largest group with 69 policies, followed by Only listed uses with 17 and Encourage with 10. Only 3 policies allow AI with conditions, 2 require something when AI is used, 1 leaves the decision to faculty, and none prohibits AI.

stances.restrict: The 17 Only listed uses policies limit which AI tools staff adopt and which decisions AI may make. Before the course, staff ensure that AI vendor contracts include data protection, privacy and security terms (P65.03, 27 universities) and acquire AI tools only through the university's standard procurement process (P65.05, 18 universities). While students work, staff ensure that AI-assisted decisions are reviewed by qualified people who can override the AI (P73.01, 12 universities), use only approved or licensed AI tools with university data (P92.08, 9 universities) and do not use AI to make final personnel or hiring decisions (P73.07, 5 universities). The one policy over time asks staff to protect ownership of research and course materials and to review the university's guidance regularly (P52.08, 6 universities).
stances.permit: All 3 Allowed with conditions policies apply while students work. Staff and their units may use AI for routine administrative tasks such as drafting emails and summarizing meetings (P76.03, 22 universities) and for institutional functions such as advising and student services, subject to authorization and privacy (P76.09, 8 universities), and they disclose how they use AI in their work (P48.06, 11 universities).
stances.encourage: The 10 Encourage policies ask staff to invest in AI, and 9 of them apply before the course. Three are each stated by 5 universities, and they ask staff to fund AI infrastructure, subscriptions and pilot programs (P122.01), to provide students with no-cost or affordable AI tools (P51.23) and to require students to take AI literacy courses or workshops (P70.03). Others recommend an AI research center (P122.02, 3 universities), new AI certificate programs (P122.04, 2 universities) and a designated referral point where students can reach human help (P72.01, 3 universities). The one policy over time asks staff to promote interdisciplinary AI research (P122.09, 2 universities).
stances.require: Both Require policies apply before the course. Staff evaluate and test AI systems for bias and fairness before deploying them (P98.03, 4 universities) and set up disclosure requirements for AI use (P24.02, 3 universities).
stances.delegates: The one Instructor decides policy states a background fact, reported by 25 universities, that the university sets no single AI policy and leaves decisions about AI use to faculty (P04.14).
stances.none: The 69 Duties and facts policies give staff the work of governing AI, and 30 of them apply before the course. The most widespread asks staff to review AI tools for security, privacy and compliance before approving them (P65.02, 65 universities), and others ask them to ensure that AI systems comply with laws and university policies (P77.02, 18 universities), to set and communicate AI expectations for faculty and students (P09.01, 17 universities) and to establish standing AI committees (P54.11, 14 universities). Over time, staff regularly reassess deployed AI systems for performance, accuracy and security (P98.06, 18 universities) and track AI's effect on student learning (P55.01, 13 universities). When misuse is suspected, the policies set a standard of proof for misconduct findings (P69.09, 5 universities) and ask staff to provide channels for reporting and redress (P71.06, 5 universities).

course.intro: Only 2 CS course policies address course staff, and both apply while students work. Each is stated by a single university. One is an Only listed uses policy and the other a Duties and facts policy, and no course policy for staff prohibits, allows, encourages or requires AI use.

stances.restrict: One syllabus reserves solution-specific debugging help for course staff (CT09.c05, 1 university).
stances.none: One syllabus lets course staff review students' AI session transcripts (CT38.c07, 1 university).

inst.intro: The 168 university, school and department policies addressed to everyone apply mostly while students work (92 policies) or state background facts (46). The other stages hold few policies, with 10 before the course, 1 during assessment, 10 when misuse is suspected and 9 over time, and none at the start of the course. By stance, Duties and facts is the largest group with 88 policies, followed by Only listed uses with 46. Thirteen policies prohibit uses of AI, 13 allow AI with conditions, 6 encourage it and 2 require something when AI is used.

stances.prohibit: The 13 prohibitions forbid using AI for harmful, deceptive or infringing ends, and 11 of them apply while students work. The most widespread asks everyone to comply with copyright law and not to use AI to infringe it (P52.11, 48 universities). Others forbid using AI to create malware or phishing (P74.01, 13 universities) or for illegal or fraudulent activity (P74.10, 11 universities), and ask people to avoid using AI to deceive others, including with fraudulent deepfakes (P74.12, 9 universities). One prohibition applies during assessment and bans autonomous AI agents, treating their use to complete assessments as cheating (P07.09, 2 universities), and one background policy says not to list AI tools as authors (P96.03, 10 universities).
stances.restrict: The 46 Only listed uses policies limit what data goes into AI tools, which tools people use and who makes final decisions, and 38 of them apply while students work. The 2 most widespread forbid entering confidential, sensitive or personally identifiable data into AI tools (P50.04, 126 universities) and allow sensitive data only in tools approved for that data type (P50.05, 104 universities). Others ask people to use only university-approved AI tools signed in with a university account (P92.05, 52 universities) and to keep final authority over important decisions that AI only supports (P73.02, 30 universities). Before the course, 63 universities require IT or governance approval before anyone acquires or uses an AI tool that is not already approved (P65.01).
stances.permit: The most widespread of the 13 Allowed with conditions policies asks people to be transparent about their AI use and to disclose or label AI-generated content (P24.06, 90 universities). Researchers may use AI for tasks such as drafting, coding and analysis (P62.07, 16 universities), anyone may use it to create accessible materials such as alt text and captions (P97.07, 8 universities), and people need not disclose AI used for minor, routine tasks like grammar editing (P100.09, 5 universities). Nine of the 13 apply while students work, and the other 4 are background statements, such as that approved disability accommodations are not restricted by AI rules (P51.24, 5 universities).
stances.encourage: The 6 Encourage policies concern AI skills, and the most widespread asks people to attend AI training and workshops (P70.11, 15 universities). Others ask people to learn prompt engineering (P93.13, 7 universities) and to structure prompts with a role, task, context and format (P93.06, 5 universities). Three of the 6 apply while students work and 3 over time.
stances.require: The 2 Require policies ask everyone to complete required AI training, often every year or at onboarding (P70.13, 11 universities), and to document AI-derived code sections along with who reviewed them (P27.05, 1 university).
stances.none: Of the 88 Duties and facts policies, the largest group, 39 state background facts and 30 apply while students work. The most widespread policy for everyone says that existing university policies and laws apply to AI use (P77.09, 145 universities), and the next asks people to critically review AI output for accuracy before relying on it (P31.03, 120 universities). The background facts warn that AI tools may store, reuse or train on what people enter (P50.14, 109 universities) and that AI models reflect and can amplify biases from their training data (P53.04, 63 universities). When misuse is suspected, people immediately report suspected data breaches or security incidents involving AI tools to the designated office (P71.03, 19 universities).

course.intro: Of the 30 CS course policies addressed to everyone, 29 state background facts and context and 1 applies at the start of the course. Duties and facts accounts for 25 of the 30. The remaining 5 are spread across Allowed with conditions (2), Prohibit (1), Only listed uses (1) and Require (1). Most are stated by few universities, and only 5 are stated by more than 5.

stances.prohibit: The one Prohibit policy states that using generative AI for assignments counts as cheating or misconduct under the integrity policy (CT36.c07, 8 universities).
stances.restrict: The one Only listed uses policy treats AI use like help from a collaborator, under the collaboration policy (CT33.c02, 6 universities).
stances.permit: The 2 Allowed with conditions policies treat AI use like the use of other online resources (CT33.c03, 3 universities) and acknowledge that AI has legitimate uses (CT04.c13, 1 university).
stances.require: In the one Require policy, the instructor discloses their own use of generative AI at the start of the course and expects students to do the same (CT25.c16, 1 university).
stances.none: The 25 Duties and facts policies describe what AI does to learning and what is wrong with its output. The most widespread say that AI output and code can be wrong, hallucinated or misleading (CT42.c01, 14 universities), that relying on AI for homework leaves students unprepared for exams (CT43.c01, 10 universities) and that AI use hinders students' own critical and independent thinking (CT40.c02, 7 universities). Others raise ethical costs, such as AI's energy and water use (CT46.c11, 2 universities), and note that employers assess job candidates without AI (CT44.c02, 5 universities).
